summary: This Wikipedia-derived note surveys Islamism as a political movement, tracing its key thinkers and organizations from Sayyid Abul Ala Maududi and Hassan al-Banna to Ali Shariati and Ruhollah Khomeini. It distinguishes moderate, democratic Islamist parties from violent radical groups such as al-Qaeda and the Taliban, and notes the debate over whether Islam is inherently political. It also links the rise of Islamist movements to the decline of secular Arab nationalism after the Six-Day War.
one_line: Overview of Islamism: its key figures, organizations, moderate and radical branches, and the debate over whether Islam is inherently political.
key_facts: Sayyid Abul Ala Maududi founded the Jamaat-e-Islami party in 1941 and remained its leader until 1972.
Maududi had more impact through his writing than through his political organising, and his books were translated into many languages.
Al-Faruqi's "Islamization of Knowledge" carried forward some of Maududi's key principles.
Hassan al Banna founded the Muslim Brotherhood in Ismailiyah, Egypt in 1928.
The Muslim Brotherhood's motto was "the Qur'an is our constitution."
Al Banna believed in government rule based on Shariah law implemented gradually and by persuasion, and in eliminating all imperialist influence in the Muslim world.
Khomeini believed complete imitation of the Prophet Mohammad and his successors such as Ali was essential for restoring Sharia law.
Khomeini held that many secular, Westernizing Muslims were actually agents of the West serving Western interests.
Ennahda Movement in Tunisia is cited as an example of a moderate reformist Islamist party that works within the democratic process.
Hezbollah in Lebanon and Hamas in Palestine participate in democratic politics as well as armed attacks, seeking to abolish the state of Israel.
Al-Qaeda, the Egyptian Islamic Jihad, and the Taliban entirely reject democracy and call for violent or offensive jihad.
Fred Halliday, John Esposito and Javed Ahmad Ghamidi are among scholars who do not believe Islam is merely a political ideology.
Hayri Abaza argues that failing to distinguish Islam from Islamism leads many in the West to support illiberal Islamic regimes.
The quick and decisive defeat of Arab troops in the Six-Day War by Israeli troops was a pivotal event in the Arab Muslim world.
After the Six-Day War, secular, socialist and nationalist politics declined in popularity, and Islamist movements inspired by Maududi and Sayyid Qutb gained ground.

entities.name: Sayyid Abul Ala Maududi
entities.role: Early twentieth-century figure in the Islamic revival in India and then Pakistan; founder of Jamaat-e-Islami in 1941 and influential writer on Islam

entities.name: Jamaat-e-Islami
entities.role: Party founded by Maududi in 1941; in Pakistan described as a socio-political and democratic Vanguard party that has also gained influence through military coup d'état

entities.name: al-Faruqi
entities.role: Liberal modernizer Islamist whose "Islamization of Knowledge" carried forward some of Maududi's principles

entities.name: Ali Shariati

entities.name: Mohammad Iqbal
entities.role: Ideological father of the State of Pakistan

entities.name: Khomeini

entities.name: Ennahda Movement
entities.role: Tunisian moderate reformist Islamist party that accepts and works within the democratic process

entities.name: Hezbollah
entities.role: Islamist group in Lebanon participating in democratic politics as well as armed attacks

entities.name: Hamas
